title: Lesson Plan — Motion in a Plane
subject: NIOS Senior Secondary Physics
objectives: Distinguish scalar and vector quantities and classify common physical quantities accordingly.
Resolve a vector into perpendicular components and apply the triangle / parallelogram law to find a resultant.
Apply the projectile-motion equations to compute time of flight, maximum height and range, and recognise the parabolic trajectory.
Explain why uniform circular motion is accelerated motion and compute the centripetal acceleration and force in mechanical scenarios.
Use relative velocity in 2D to solve river-crossing and crosswind problems.
prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion and force diagrams (Chapter 3).
Trigonometry: sine, cosine, tangent of standard angles.
materials: Whiteboard with two-coloured markers (one for x-motion, one for y-motion).
Length of light string with a small weight (for whirling-stone demo).
Two metre rulers (to draw vectors to scale).
Stopwatch and a tennis ball (for the projectile demo).

activities.description: Throw-and-predict: the teacher tosses a tennis ball across the room at two different angles (about 30° and 60°) at the same throw-strength. Class is asked to predict (i) which throw lands further, (ii) which stays in the air longer, (iii) which goes higher.
teacher_actions: Throw the ball at roughly the same speed at two contrasting angles.
Promise that the projectile equations will tell us who is right by the end of the lesson.
student_actions: Watch carefully and predict in pairs.
Justify the prediction briefly (which angle is best for distance, which for hang time).

activities.description: Vector recap with arrows: students work in pairs to draw any 2D vector as an arrow and read off its components A_x and A_y for two given angles (30°, 60°). They then add a second arrow head-to-tail and measure the resultant with a ruler.
teacher_actions: Provide a small handout with grid paper.
Circulate and check that students are drawing tail-to-head, not tail-to-tail.
Highlight that the resultant goes from the FREE tail to the FREE head.
student_actions: Draw two vectors of given magnitudes/angles to scale.
Compute A_x = A cos θ and A_y = A sin θ for each.
Add the two vectors graphically and measure |R|; compare with the cosine-rule answer.

activities.description: Direct instruction on the three big ideas of the chapter: (i) component decoupling — 2D motion under constant a splits into two independent 1D problems; (ii) projectile motion equations T, H, R and the parabolic trajectory; (iii) uniform circular motion — why it is accelerated motion and where the centripetal force comes from in different scenarios.
teacher_actions: Use two-colour board work (one colour for x-motion, one for y-motion) to drive home decoupling.
Derive T, H, R from u_x = u cos θ, u_y = u sin θ.
Whirl the string-and-weight at the front of the class; ask 'what would happen if the string broke?'
Emphasise that centripetal force is not a new fundamental force — it has different physical sources in different situations.
student_actions: Take notes using the same two-colour convention.
Predict (and then verify) that the stone flies off tangentially when the string is released.
Identify the centripetal-force source in each example: tension, gravity, friction, normal.

activities.description: Two worked examples + one open-ended problem: (a) projectile launched at 20 m/s at 30° — find T, H, R; (b) car on a flat unbanked curve — find max safe speed for given μ and r; (c) open: a boat (5 m/s) crosses a river (3 m/s) 100 m wide — discuss both shortest-time and shortest-path strategies and which is appropriate.
teacher_actions: Model the projectile problem on the board step by step, then have students solve a sibling problem on their own.
Pose the boat problem and let students argue in pairs about which heading is right.
Take a vote and then walk through the answer.
student_actions: Solve the practice projectile problem individually.
Discuss boat strategy in pairs, then defend their answer to the class.
Compute t_min and t_path and compare.

activities.description: Quick check: a 5-question MCQ exit ticket covering scalar vs vector, projectile range formula, centripetal-force source identification, and relative velocity. Students hand in slips on the way out.
teacher_actions: Project the 5 MCQs on the board.
Walk around to spot misconceptions on the fly.
Note any consistent wrong answers to revisit in the next lesson.
student_actions: Answer all 5 questions on a slip.
Star any question they were unsure about, so the teacher knows where to recap.

activities.description: Homework: complete the chapter worksheet (12 questions, mix of objective and subjective) and revisit the opening demo predictions — did they match the formulas?
teacher_actions: Remind students that the worksheet's answer key is available after they have attempted it.
student_actions: Read through the worksheet questions before leaving so they can clarify doubts immediately.
Attempt at home and bring questions to the next class.

homework: Re-derive R = u² sin 2θ / g from first principles (without referring to notes).
Find one real-life example (other than the ones in class) of uniform circular motion and identify the centripetal-force source.
assessment_ideas: 5-question MCQ exit ticket at the end of the lesson.
End-of-chapter test combining 10 objective + 2 subjective + 1 case-based question.
Practical: have students compute the optimum launch angle for their own throw and verify in a schoolyard experiment with a stopwatch and a measuring tape.
references: NIOS Senior Secondary Physics, Lesson 4: Motion in a Plane.
NCERT Class 11 Physics, Chapter 4: Motion in a Plane.
HC Verma, Concepts of Physics Vol. 1, Chapter 3 (Rest and Motion: Kinematics).
